title: Sequences & nth Term
description: Linear sequences, position-to-term rules, and a first look at quadratic sequences for MYP 3.

notes.heading: Linear Sequences

illustration.alt: A linear sequence shown as numbered steps with position numbers 1 to 5 and terms 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, connected by arrows labelled plus 3.
illustration.caption: A linear sequence has a constant common difference between consecutive terms.

notes.body:
📌 Definition
A linear sequence is a sequence in which the difference between consecutive terms is always the same. This fixed difference is called the common difference.

    $$4, 7, 10, 13, 16, \dots$$

    The common difference is $7 - 4 = 3$.

🔑 Key Concept
Because the pattern grows by equal steps, plotting position $n$ against term value gives points that lie on a straight line.

💡 Worked Example
Find the common difference of $15, 11, 7, 3, -1, \dots$.

  $11 - 15 = -4$
  $7 - 11 = -4$
  $3 - 7 = -4$

  The common difference is $-4$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A linear sequence is also called an arithmetic sequence.
• The common difference can be positive or negative.
• Check at least two differences before deciding a sequence is linear.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Calling any sequence with a pattern 'linear'. A sequence is linear only when the first differences are constant.

notes.heading: Position-to-Term Rules
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A position-to-term rule is a formula that gives the value of any term directly from its position number $n$.

    We often write the $n$th term as $T_n$ or $u_n$.

🔑 Key Concept
For a linear sequence with common difference $d$ and first term $a$, the $n$th term can be written as:

    $$T_n = a + (n - 1)d$$

    A quicker form for many calculations is:

    $$T_n = dn + c$$

    where $d$ is the common difference and $c$ is a constant chosen to make the first term correct.

💡 Worked Example
The $n$th term of a sequence is $T_n = 5n - 2$. Find the first four terms.

  $T_1 = 5(1) - 2 = 3$
  $T_2 = 5(2) - 2 = 8$
  $T_3 = 5(3) - 2 = 13$
  $T_4 = 5(4) - 2 = 18$

  The sequence is $3, 8, 13, 18, \dots$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Substitute $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ to generate terms.
• The number multiplying $n$ is the common difference.
• The rule works for any term, however large $n$ is.

✅ Check
For $T_n = 5n - 2$, the common difference should be $5$. The terms $3, 8, 13, 18$ increase by $5$ each time, so the rule is correct.

notes.heading: Finding the nth Term of a Linear Sequence
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
1. Find the common difference $d$.
2. Start the rule with $dn$.
3. Substitute $n = 1$ and compare with the first term to find the constant $c$.

💡 Worked Example
Find the $n$th term of $6, 10, 14, 18, 22, \dots$.

  Step 1: Common difference
    $10 - 6 = 4$, so $d = 4$.

  Step 2: Start with $4n$.

  Step 3: Find $c$
    When $n = 1$, $4n = 4$, but the first term is $6$.
    $c = 6 - 4 = 2$.

  The $n$th term is:
    $$T_n = 4n + 2$$

  ✅ Check: For $n = 4$, $4(4) + 2 = 18$ ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The coefficient of $n$ is always the common difference.
• To find $c$, work out first term minus $d$.
• Always test the rule on at least two terms.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting that $c$ is not the first term. For $6, 10, 14, \dots$, the first term is $6$ but the rule is $4n + 2$, not $4n + 6$.

notes.heading: Using the nth Term
notes.body:
🔑 Key Concept
Once you have the $n$th term, you can answer many questions without listing every term.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Find a far term
The $n$th term of a sequence is $T_n = 7n - 3$. Find the $50$th term.

  $$T_{50} = 7(50) - 3 = 350 - 3 = 347$$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Is a number in the sequence?
Is $92$ a term of the sequence with $n$th term $T_n = 6n + 2$?

  Set $6n + 2 = 92$.
  $6n = 90$
  $n = 15$

  Since $n = 15$ is a whole number, $92$ is the $15$th term.

💡 Worked Example 3 — Find which term equals a value
Which term of $T_n = 8n - 5$ equals $91$?

  $8n - 5 = 91$
  $8n = 96$
  $n = 12$

  The $12$th term is $91$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Set the $n$th term equal to the target value and solve for $n$.
• If $n$ is not a positive whole number, the value is not in the sequence.
• Always interpret your answer in the context of the question.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Assuming every whole-number answer means the value is in the sequence. The value must also match the sequence direction; for example, $n = 0$ or negative $n$ are not valid positions.

notes.heading: Introduction to Quadratic Sequences
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A quadratic sequence is a sequence whose $n$th term includes an $n^2$ part. The second differences between terms are constant.

🔑 Key Concept
For the simplest quadratic sequence, the square numbers:

    $$T_n = n^2$$

    the terms are $1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, \dots$.

    First differences: $3, 5, 7, 9, 11$
    Second differences: $2, 2, 2, 2$

    The constant second difference tells us the sequence is quadratic.

💡 Worked Example
Write the first five terms of $T_n = n^2 + 2$.

  $T_1 = 1^2 + 2 = 3$
  $T_2 = 2^2 + 2 = 6$
  $T_3 = 3^2 + 2 = 11$
  $T_4 = 4^2 + 2 = 18$
  $T_5 = 5^2 + 2 = 27$

  The sequence is $3, 6, 11, 18, 27, \dots$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Quadratic sequences grow faster than linear sequences.
• The $n$th term always contains $n^2$ (or a multiple of $n^2$).
• Second differences being constant is the signature of a quadratic sequence.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Trying to fit a linear rule to a quadratic sequence. If the first differences are not constant, check the second differences before giving up on a simple rule.

notes.heading: Finding Simple Quadratic nth Terms
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
For MYP 3 we focus on quadratic rules of the form $T_n = an^2 + c$.

1. Compare the sequence with $n^2$.
2. Decide whether each term is multiplied by a number or shifted up/down.
3. Test your rule on at least two terms.

💡 Worked Example 1
Find the $n$th term of $2, 8, 18, 32, 50, \dots$.

  Compare with $n^2$: $1, 4, 9, 16, 25$.
  Each given term is double the corresponding square number.

  $$T_n = 2n^2$$

  Check: $2(3)^2 = 18$ ✓

💡 Worked Example 2
Find the $n$th term of $5, 8, 13, 20, 29, \dots$.

  Compare with $n^2$: $1, 4, 9, 16, 25$.
  Each term is $4$ more than the corresponding square number.

  $$T_n = n^2 + 4$$

  Check: $3^2 + 4 = 13$ ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• If terms are multiples of square numbers, the rule is $an^2$.
• If terms are square numbers shifted by a constant, the rule is $n^2 + c$.
• Always check by substituting $n = 1, 2, 3$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing $2n^2$ with $(2n)^2$. They are different: $2n^2$ means $2 \times n^2$, while $(2n)^2 = 4n^2$.

notes.heading: Solving Problems with Sequences
notes.body:
🔑 Key Concept
Many real situations follow a linear or quadratic pattern. Identify the type of sequence, find the rule, and then use it to answer the question.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Linear pattern
A staircase has steps. Step $1$ uses $5$ bricks, Step $2$ uses $8$ bricks, Step $3$ uses $11$ bricks, and the pattern continues. How many bricks are needed for Step $20$?

  Sequence: $5, 8, 11, \dots$
  Common difference: $3$
  First term: $5$

  $T_n = 3n + 2$

  $$T_{20} = 3(20) + 2 = 62$$

  Step $20$ needs $62$ bricks.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Quadratic pattern
The number of tiles in a growing pattern is $2, 6, 12, 20, 30, \dots$. Find the $n$th term.

  Compare with $n^2$: $1, 4, 9, 16, 25$.
  Each term is the square number plus its position number.

  $$T_n = n^2 + n$$

  Check: $3^2 + 3 = 12$ ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Read the problem to find the first term and the pattern of growth.
• Decide whether the pattern is linear (constant first difference) or quadratic (constant second difference).
• Write the rule before substituting a large value.

✅ Check
After finding a rule, generate the first three terms mentally and compare them with the question to catch sign or arithmetic errors.

flashcards.definition: A sequence with a constant difference between consecutive terms.
The fixed amount added or subtracted between consecutive terms of a linear sequence.
A formula that gives any term directly from its position number $n$.
The formula for a sequence written using the position number $n$.
For a linear sequence, $T_n = dn + c$, where $d$ is the common difference.
The term in position $1$ of a sequence, often denoted $a$ or $T_1$.
Find the common difference, start with $dn$, then add a constant so the first term is correct.

flashcards.term: Checking if a number is in a sequence
flashcards.definition: Set the nth term equal to the number and solve for $n$. If $n$ is a positive whole number, the number is in the sequence.
flashcards.example: For $T_n = 4n + 3$, set $47 = 4n + 3$ to get $n = 11$, so $47$ is the $11$th term.

flashcards.definition: A sequence whose nth term includes $n^2$ and whose second differences are constant.
The difference between consecutive first differences of a sequence.
flashcards.example: For $n^2$: first differences are $3, 5, 7, 9$, so second differences are $2, 2, 2$.

flashcards.definition: A quadratic rule of the form $T_n = an^2 + c$ for MYP 3.
A shorthand for the term in position $n$ of a sequence.

questions.stem: What is the next term in the linear sequence $7, 12, 17, 22, 27, \dots$?
questions.explanation: The common difference is $5$, since $12 - 7 = 5$. Therefore, $27 + 5 = 32$.

questions.stem: Find the common difference of the sequence $20, 16, 12, 8, 4, \dots$.
questions.explanation: Each term is $4$ less than the previous term: $16 - 20 = -4$, $12 - 16 = -4$, and so on.

questions.stem: What is the $n$th term of the sequence $3, 7, 11, 15, 19, \dots$?
questions.explanation: The common difference is $4$, so start with $4n$. When $n = 1$, $4n = 4$, but the first term is $3$, so subtract $1$. The rule is $4n - 1$.

questions.stem: The $n$th term of a sequence is $T_n = 6n - 5$. What is the $10$th term?
Find the $n$th term of the sequence $9, 14, 19, 24, 29, \dots$.
questions.explanation: The common difference is $5$, so start with $5n$. When $n = 1$, $5n = 5$, but the first term is $9$, so add $4$. The rule is $5n + 4$.

questions.stem: The $n$th term of a sequence is $T_n = 8n + 3$. Which term equals $75$?
questions.explanation: Set $8n + 3 = 75$. Subtract $3$ to get $8n = 72$, then divide by $8$ to get $n = 9$.

questions.stem: Is $50$ a term of the sequence with $n$th term $T_n = 6n + 2$?
choices: No, because $n$ is not a whole number
questions.explanation: Set $6n + 2 = 50$. Subtract $2$ to get $6n = 48$, then divide by $6$ to get $n = 8$. So $50$ is the $8$th term.

questions.stem: Find the missing term in the linear sequence $10, 17, \underline{\quad}, 31, 38$.
questions.explanation: The common difference is $7$, since $17 - 10 = 7$ and $38 - 31 = 7$. Therefore, $17 + 7 = 24$, and checking, $24 + 7 = 31$.

questions.stem: A taxi fare starts at ＄4 and increases by ＄3 for each kilometre travelled. How much does a $15$ km journey cost?
questions.explanation: The cost sequence is $7, 10, 13, \dots$, with first term $7$ and common difference $3$. The $n$th term is $T_n = 3n + 4$. For $15$ km, $T_{15} = 3(15) + 4 = 49$, so the fare is ＄49.

questions.stem: What is the next term in the quadratic sequence $2, 5, 10, 17, 26, \dots$?
questions.explanation: The sequence follows $T_n = n^2 + 1$, since $1^2 + 1 = 2$, $2^2 + 1 = 5$, and so on. The $6$th term is $6^2 + 1 = 37$.

questions.stem: What is the $n$th term of the quadratic sequence $3, 6, 11, 18, 27, \dots$?
questions.explanation: Compare with $n^2$: $1, 4, 9, 16, 25$. Each term is $2$ more than the corresponding square number, so the rule is $T_n = n^2 + 2$.

questions.stem: What is the second difference of the square-number sequence $1, 4, 9, 16, 25, \dots$?
questions.explanation: First differences are $3, 5, 7, 9$. The second differences are $5 - 3 = 2$, $7 - 5 = 2$, and $9 - 7 = 2$, so the second difference is $2$.

questions.stem: Find the $n$th term of the sequence $22, 17, 12, 7, 2, \dots$.
questions.explanation: The common difference is $-5$. Starting with $-5n$, when $n = 1$ we get $-5$, but the first term is $22$, so we need $27 - 5n$. Check: $27 - 5(2) = 17$ ✓.

questions.stem: A tile pattern has $2$ tiles in Picture $1$, $6$ tiles in Picture $2$, $12$ tiles in Picture $3$, and $20$ tiles in Picture $4$. How many tiles are in Picture $5$?
questions.explanation: The sequence is $2, 6, 12, 20$. Comparing with $n^2$: $1, 4, 9, 16$, each term is $n^2 + n$. For Picture $5$, $5^2 + 5 = 25 + 5 = 30$.

questions.stem: Which of these sequences is quadratic?
questions.explanation: $2, 5, 10, 17, 26$ has first differences $3, 5, 7, 9$ and constant second difference $2$, so it follows $T_n = n^2 + 1$ and is quadratic.
